Then he does something a reader can learn a great deal from — he shows that this is not an isolated claim but a refrain running right through the Qur'an, and he lines the verses up:

- *"Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better"* — the words of those who were given knowledge (28:80)
- *"And what is with Allah for the righteous is better"* (3:198)
- *"Although the Hereafter is better and enduring"* (87:17)

And then the one Ibn Kathir points out was said by Allah to His Messenger ﷺ himself: *"And indeed the Hereafter is better for you than the present"* (93:4). If the Prophet ﷺ — of all people — was told that what is coming is better than what he had, then this is not a consolation prize offered to people who lost out in this world. It is a statement about the real order of things.

**"And excellent indeed will be the home of those who have taqwa."** Ibn Kathir treats this as the passage's turn toward describing the abode itself — which is exactly what ayah 31 then does.

## Ayah 31: what the home actually is

**Gardens of ʿAdn — Gardens of Eternity.** Ibn Kathir identifies these as the home of the *muttaqūn*, the people of taqwa: in the Hereafter they will have Gardens of Eternity **in which they will dwell forever.** Permanence is built into the name. Everything else the ayah lists sits inside that permanence — which is what makes it unlike every good thing in this world, all of which we hold knowing we will one day let go.

**"Under which rivers flow."** Ibn Kathir gives a beautifully concrete gloss: the rivers run **between its trees and its palaces.** Not a distant landscape feature — water threading through the place where they actually live.

**"In it they will have all that they wish."** Ibn Kathir pairs this with:

> *"In it there will be all that souls could desire, and all that eyes could delight in, and in it you will live forever."* (43:71)

Read the two together and you get the full shape of it: what the soul desires from within, what the eye delights in from without, and time enough that neither ever ends. The ayah does not enumerate the pleasures — it simply hands over the criterion. Whatever *they* wish.

**"Thus Allah rewards those who have taqwa."** Ibn Kathir's comment here is important, because it defines who this passage is actually about. It means, he says, **this is how Allah rewards everyone who believes in Him, fears Him, and does good deeds.**

That is a working description of the person in three parts: belief in Allah, fear of Him, and action. Not fear alone, which can curdle; not belief alone, which can go inert; not good deeds alone, which can float free of their Owner. All three, together, in one person. That is the person ayah 30 puts the question to, and the person ayah 31 hands the Gardens to.

## Ayah 32: the moment at the door

Having shown the destination, the passage rewinds to the doorway. Ibn Kathir introduces ayah 32 as telling us about the believers' condition **when death approaches them in a good state.**

The Arabic word for that state is **ṭayyibīn** — the translation renders it "while they are virtuous," and Ibn Kathir spells out what it means: **free from shirk, from impurity, and from all evil.** Read carefully, that is a description of a condition a person is *in*, not a tally of things they have done. The ayah pictures the angels arriving and finding them like that.

Then the angels speak. Two sentences, and they contain everything:

**"Salāmun ʿalaykum" — peace be upon you.** A greeting of peace, spoken to the believer by the angels who take his soul. Whatever the appearance of the deathbed to those standing around it, the words actually being spoken there are words of peace.

**"Enter Paradise because of what you used to do."** The wording is habitual — not what you did once, but what you *used to do*, the settled pattern of a life. Deeds that were repeated until they were simply who you were. And note that the invitation is not to hope, or to wait, or to be judged: *enter*.

Ibn Kathir places alongside this the fullest picture the Qur'an gives of that moment:

> *"Verily, those who say: 'Our Lord is Allah,' and then behave righteously, on them the angels will descend, saying: 'Fear not, nor grieve! But receive the good news of Paradise as you have been promised! We have been your friends in the life of this world and are so in the Hereafter. In it you shall have all that your souls desire, and in it you shall have all that you ask for. An entertainment from the Oft-Forgiving, Most Merciful.'"* (41:30–32)

Look at what those angels say about themselves: *we have been your friends in the life of this world.* The believer, it turns out, was never walking alone. The companionship that becomes visible at death had been there the whole time, unseen. And notice the two fears the angels address by name — *do not fear* what is coming, *do not grieve* what you are leaving. Death touches a person from both directions, and the angels' greeting meets both.

Ibn Kathir closes by noting that the hadiths reported on the taking of the soul of the believer and the soul of the disbeliever were already discussed under the ayah *"Allah will keep firm those who believe, with the word that stands firm in this world (i.e. they will keep on worshipping Allah Alone and none else), and in the Hereafter. And Allah will cause the wrongdoers to stray, and Allah does as He wills."* (14:27). He is pointing the reader to where that detail lives rather than repeating it — and so, since those reports are not set out here, they are not set out here either. What the pairing does show is that Ibn Kathir sees the believer's death and the firmness Allah grants His believing servants as one subject.

## Living it

**Answer the question honestly, and answer it now.** Ayah 30 asks what you say your Lord has sent down. The believers' answer is not clever — it is one word. But Ibn Kathir's gloss shows what stands behind it: something good has come down, and it is mercy and blessing *for those who followed it and believed in it.* You only speak that way about a book you have actually let into your life.

**Watch what you say about the Qur'an in front of others.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's account of the deniers is not only about them denying — it is about them spreading the denial, and carrying part of the evil consequence of everyone they turned away. Speech about revelation is never private; it lands on other people, and it is weighed.

**Take the two-part promise seriously.** Ibn Kathir is explicit that the good of ayah 30 reaches a person in this world and in the next, and that the reward in the Hereafter is the more complete of the two. A believer is not asked to write off this life as loss. He is asked to rank it correctly — the Hereafter is *better*, as Allah told even His own Messenger ﷺ.

**Aim at the state, not just the acts.** Ayah 32 does not say the angels take those who did much, but those who are *ṭayyibīn* — free of shirk, of impurity, of evil. Since none of us chooses the hour, that has to be the ordinary condition of a life rather than something arranged at the end.

**And let the ending shape the middle.** The last words the believer hears in this world, in this passage, are *peace be upon you* and *enter*. Everything ayat 30–32 describe in between — the answer given, the good done, the fear of Allah kept — is simply the road to that sentence.

passages.title: Awaiting the angels or Allah's decree
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat pose a question that is not really a question: *what, exactly, are these people waiting for?* Ayah 33 names the two comings they are in fact awaiting — the angels, or the command of their Lord — and points to those before them, who did the same. Ayah 34 states what then befell them. The two ayat are one movement: the waiting, and the arrival.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the scene. The surah has been describing the blessings of Allah and proving that He alone is unique in the creation of the universe — and then it makes a pointed reference to how the polytheists chose to stick to their own ways of error. In these present ayat, the text describes how they were not content with their own straying: they tried to make others go astray like them. The punishment they would get for doing that is part of what is stated here.

Earlier, at ayah 24, a question was put about the Qur'an, and the ones being addressed there were the polytheists. Their answer was haughty and ignorant: they simply refused to acknowledge that any word of Allah had really been revealed from Him, and dismissed the Qur'an as nothing but tales of people from early ages. Maʿārif notes that the Qur'an does not explicitly say who asked that question, and commentators have expressed different views — some say the question was asked by disbelievers, some by Muslims, some take one question to have come from the polytheists and the other from Muslims. But the Qur'an has kept it ambiguous, and Maʿārif draws the lesson from that: there is no need to ask where the question came from. What has to be seen is the answer and, more importantly, its ultimate consequence — which the Qur'an has itself chosen to describe. Then, after five ayat, at ayah 30, the same question is addressed to believers who fear Allah; their answer follows, and with it a promise of reward.

So our passage is the other side of that ledger. Ayat 33–34 are where the polytheists' answer meets its consequence.

## "Are they but waiting…?" (ayah 33)

The wording is "Are they but waiting for the angels to come to them, or there comes the command of your Lord?" — a question with only one answer left in it.

Ibn Kathir reads the ayah as a threat issued to the idolaters for their persistence in falsehood and their conceited delusions about this world. He puts the heading over it plainly: the disbelievers' refrain from faith means that they were simply awaiting punishment. Notice what that framing does. Their refusal to believe is not described as a considered position. It is described as a waiting — and what is on its way is named for them.

## The two arrivals

**"That the angels come to them."** Ibn Kathir explains this directly: are these people waiting only for the angels to come and take their souls?

**"Or there comes the command of your Lord."** Here Ibn Kathir cites Qatadah, who said this means the Day of Resurrection and the terror that they will go through.

Two comings, then, and both are named in the ayah itself.

## "Thus did those before them"

Ibn Kathir explains: this means that their predecessors, and those who were like them among the idolaters, persisted in their *shirk* — idolatry, the setting up of others alongside Allah — until they tasted the wrath of Allah and experienced the punishment and torment that they suffered.

The question of ayah 33 is not left hanging in theory. The ayah points to people who already stood where these people stand, and says plainly how it ended for them.

## "And Allah did not wrong them"

This is the moral centre of the passage, and it is stated with great care. Ibn Kathir explains: Allah did not wrong them **because by sending His Messengers and revealing His Books He gave them enough warning and clearly demonstrated His proofs to them.** Nothing arrived without notice. The messengers came, the books came, the proofs were made plain. Justice here means the case was fully made before the sentence fell.

Then the ayah relocates the wrongdoing: **"but they were wronging themselves."** Ibn Kathir: that is, by opposing the Messengers and denying what they brought — and for this reason Allah's punishment tormented them. The injury never travelled from Allah to them. It travelled from them to themselves.

## What arrived (ayah 34)

**"Then the evil consequences of what they did overtook them."** The ayah does not say that some unrelated calamity struck them. It says the evils *of what they did* struck them — Ibn Kathir renders it as their being afflicted by their evil deeds.

**"And they were surrounded by that which they used to mock."** On *wa ḥāqa bihim* — "they were surrounded" — Ibn Kathir says: they were overwhelmed by the painful torment. Two words stand side by side here: the ayah's *surrounded*, and Ibn Kathir's *overwhelmed*. And what is it that comes upon them? The very thing they used to mock.

Ibn Kathir spells out what that mockery was: they used to make fun of the Messengers when they warned them of Allah's punishment. And for this, he says, it will be said to them on the Day of Resurrection: **"This is the Fire which you used to belie"** (52:14). What they made light of is exactly what is named to them on that Day.

## Living it

**Waiting is itself a posture, and the ayah answers it.** Ibn Kathir sums up the disbelievers' refrain from faith as, in effect, awaiting punishment — refusal described not as an argument but as a waiting. The ayah answers that posture on its own terms: something is indeed coming, and it names what. That is worth sitting with whenever we leave a matter open and stay comfortable.

**Mockery is not a light thing.** The passage follows one specific habit — making fun of the Messengers when they warned of Allah's punishment — all the way to its end, and the end is being surrounded by that same thing. It is worth being careful how we speak about what we do not accept, or do not yet understand, of Allah's religion.

**What you pass on to others carries weight.** Maʿārif draws this out: these people were not merely astray. They told others that the Qur'an was nothing but the tales of the ancients, and thereby made others go astray like them. The total curse of their sins has to fall on them anyway on the Day of Judgment, and in addition, part of the curse of the evil consequences of their role in misguiding others will also fall on them. The burden of sins they are piling on their own shoulders, Maʿārif says, is a terribly evil burden. Anyone who speaks publicly about Allah's Book — in a class, in a family, online — should feel the seriousness in that.

**Take Allah's justice as it is stated.** The relief in ayah 33 is not that punishment is unreal, but that it is never arbitrary. "Allah did not wrong them" is the Qur'an's own verdict on His dealing with them: Messengers sent, Books revealed, proofs clearly demonstrated. The ayah then places the wrong squarely where it belongs — "they were wronging themselves." That should leave a believer neither anxious about Allah's fairness nor casual about his own choices, but grateful that the warning came, and quick to answer it.

passages.title: 'Had Allah willed' — the fatalist excuse answered
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The idolaters had found a way to make their idolatry look like Allah's own doing: if He truly disliked what we do, they said, He would have stopped us. Ayat 35–37 dismantle that excuse — first by pointing to the messengers Allah sent to every community (ayah 36), then by turning to the Prophet ﷺ himself (ayah 37) and steadying him when such people still refuse.

What binds the three ayat into one unit is a single line of argument. They claim heaven has been silent about their behaviour; Allah replies that heaven has never been silent, not once, in any nation; and then He tells His Messenger ﷺ that when a heart still will not open after all that, the failure is not his to carry.

## The excuse itself (ayah 35)

Ibn Kathir titles this passage exactly for what it is: *the idolaters' argument that their shirk was divinely decreed, and the refutation of this claim*. (*Shirk* is the Arabic term for associating partners with Allah — directing worship to anything alongside Him.) He says Allah is telling us here about "the idolators delusion over their Shirk, and the excuse they claimed for it based on the idea that it is ordained by divine decree."

Notice that their statement has two halves, and they are not the same kind of claim:

**"Had Allah willed, neither we nor our fathers would have worshipped anything besides Him"** — this is about worship: the gods they set up alongside Allah.

**"nor would we have forbidden anything without (a command from) Him"** — this is about law: things they had declared off-limits. Ibn Kathir explains what lies behind this second half. They had superstitious customs concerning certain animals — he names the *Bahirah*, the *Sa'ibah* and the *Wasilah* — along with other practices "that they had invented and innovated by themselves, with no revealed authority." So they were not only worshipping wrongly; they were legislating, declaring things forbidden that Allah had never forbidden, and then hanging that invented law on Allah's will.

**The logic underneath.** Ibn Kathir boils their reasoning down to one sentence: *"If Allah hated what we did, He would have stopped by punishing us, and He would not have enabled us to do it."* That is the whole argument. Ability is taken as approval. The fact that we are able to do it, and that no punishment has fallen, is read as proof that He is content with it.

Notice that this is not really a theological position; it is a shrug. It takes the doctrine of divine decree — which is true — and puts it to work as a defence lawyer, which it never was. Ibn Kathir's verdict on the attempt is blunt: "there is no argument in that for them."

## The reply: "Are the messengers charged with anything but clear conveyance?"

Allah's answer at the end of ayah 35 comes as a question: **فَهَلْ عَلَى الرُّسُلِ إِلَّا الْبَلَاغُ الْمُبِينُ** — "Are the Messengers charged with anything but to clearly convey the Message?"

The phrase rendered "clearly convey the Message" is *al-balāgh al-mubīn* — delivering the message plainly, so that it arrives and is understood. Ibn Kathir unpacks the force of the question: "the matter is not as you claim. It is not the case that Allah did not rebuke your behavior; rather, He did rebuke you, and in the strongest possible terms, and He emphatically forbade you from such behavior."

So the answer to "why didn't He stop us?" is: *He did tell you to stop.* You were not left in the dark and then blamed for stumbling. The message was conveyed, and conveyed clearly — which is precisely what the messengers were charged with. The excuse "Allah never objected" dies there.

## A messenger to every community (ayah 36)

Ayah 36 turns that reply into a sweeping historical claim: **وَلَقَدْ بَعَثْنَا فِي كُلِّ أُمَّةٍ رَّسُولًا أَنِ اعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ وَاجْتَنِبُوا الطَّاغُوتَ** — "And We have indeed sent a Messenger to every Ummah (community, nation) saying: Worship Allah alone, and shun the *Taghut*."

*Ṭāghūt* is glossed in the sources as all false deities — everything set up as an object of worship beside Allah. Notice the shape of the command: one positive, one negative. *Worship Allah* — and *stay away from* what is worshipped besides Him. It is not enough to add Allah to a crowded shelf; the shelf has to be cleared.

Ibn Kathir stresses that no community was skipped: "To every nation — that is, to every generation, to every community of people — He sent a Messenger. All of the Messengers called their people to worship Allah alone as well as forbidding them from worshipping anything or anybody except for Him." He traces the line from its beginning to its end: from "the first incidence of Shirk that appeared among the Children of Adam, in the people to whom Nuh was sent — the first Messenger sent by Allah to the people of this earth — until He sent the final Messenger, Muhammad ﷺ, whose call was addressed to both men and Jinn, in the east and in the west."

And every one of them carried the identical message. Ibn Kathir cites Allah's words: *"And We did not send any Messenger before you but We revealed to him: None has the right to be worshipped but I, so worship Me"* (21:25), and *"And ask those Messengers of Ours whom We sent before you: Did We ever appoint gods to be worshipped besides the Most Gracious?"* (43:45).

Having laid that out, Ibn Kathir turns the obvious question back on them: **"So how could any of the idolators say, 'If Allah had so willed, we would not have worshipped any but Him'?"** With that many messengers, in that many nations, over that much time — on what grounds do you claim Allah never objected?

## The heart of it: two senses of "will"

This is where the passage repays careful reading, because the idolaters were not lying about the facts. Allah *did* permit their shirk to occur. Their mistake lay in what they concluded from that permission. Ibn Kathir draws the distinction that unlocks the whole passage:

> "The legislative will of Allah is clear and cannot be taken as an excuse by them, because He had forbidden them to do that upon the tongue of His Messengers, but by His universal will — by which He allows things to occur even though they do not please Him — He allowed them to do that as it was decreed for them. So there is no argument in that for them."

Two different things are being called "Allah's will":

**His legislative will** — what He has commanded and forbidden. This is public and unmistakable; it came "upon the tongue of His Messengers." Measured against this will, their idolatry was flatly, loudly against what Allah willed.

**His universal will** — His decree by which things actually come to pass. Their shirk happened, so in this sense it fell within Allah's will. But — and this is the point they missed — Ibn Kathir is explicit that this will "allows things to occur even though they do not please Him."

That is the hinge of the whole argument. *Allah permitting a thing to happen is not Allah approving of it.* The idolaters collapsed the two wills into one, and so read their own ability to sin as a licence to sin. Ibn Kathir presses the point with a stark example: "Allah created Hell and its people, both the Shayatin and disbelievers, but He does not like His servants to disbelieve." (*Shayāṭīn* — devils.) He created it; He does not love it. And he adds that this distinction "constitutes the strongest proof and the most unquestionable wisdom."

Both truths stand at once, and Ibn Kathir holds them together without collapsing either: things occur by Allah's decree, and Allah does not love disbelief in His servants. Neither truth cancels the other, and — as he concludes — there is no argument in it for anyone who wants to use the first to hide from the second.

## "Then why not simply force us?" — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states the objection in its bluntest form: "If Allah does not like our Kufr and Shirk and other unlawful deeds, why would He not stop us from doing so by force?" (*Kufr* is disbelief — the rejection of faith.)

Its first observation is about the Qur'an's own tone. The absurdity of the doubt "was all too evident. Therefore, instead of answering it, just saying words of comfort for the Holy Prophet ﷺ was considered sufficient, so that he does not feel sad about such senseless questions." That is a striking reading of ayah 37: it is not primarily a rebuttal to them at all — it is consolation to him. Some objections do not deserve an argument; the Qur'an steps past them and attends to the messenger's heart instead.

Then Maʿārif explains why the objection collapses. Allah "has set up the system of this world on the basic arrangement that human beings have not been kept under compulsion totally. A kind of power to choose was given to them. If they use this choice in obedience to Allah, they have their reward for it; and if they use it to disobey Him, then, there stands His promise of punishment."

Two things follow. First, the Day of Judgement is the natural consequence of this arrangement — Maʿārif notes that resurrection and being "called to account for their deeds are the consequential outcome of this early warning." A world of forced obedience would need no reckoning. Second, force was never withheld out of weakness: "If Allah Ta'ala had decided that He would force everyone to obey Him, who then would have dared to remain outside the fold of obedience to Him? But, His wisdom so required that such compulsion was not appropriate. Therefore, choice was given to human beings."

So the demand "stop us by force" is really a demand that Allah cancel the arrangement He deliberately made. Maʿārif's verdict on the question is plain: "It is an absurd and hostile question."

## "Travel through the land" — history as the answer

The middle of ayah 36 divides humanity by outcome: "**Then among them were some whom Allah guided, and among them were some who deserved to be left to stray.**" The messengers came to everyone; the responses parted.

And then a command that answers their excuse with evidence: **فَسِيرُوا فِي الْأَرْضِ فَانظُرُوا كَيْفَ كَانَ عَاقِبَةُ الْمُكَذِّبِينَ** — "So travel through the land and see the end of those who denied the truth."

Ibn Kathir reads this as the direct rebuttal of their claim that Allah never objected: "Then Allah informs us that He rebuked them with punishment in this world, after the Messengers issued their warning." You said He would have punished you if He disapproved — very well, go and look. Ibn Kathir cites: *"Allah destroyed them completely, and a similar end awaits the disbelievers"* (47:10), and *"And indeed those before them denied the Messengers, so how terrible was My denial"* (67:18). He explains the instruction itself as: "ask about what happened to those who went against the Messengers and rejected the truth." The evidence is not abstract; it is geography.

## Ayah 37: a word to the Prophet ﷺ

**إِن تَحْرِصْ عَلَىٰ هُدَاهُمْ فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ لَا يَهْدِي مَن يُضِلُّ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن نَّاصِرِينَ** — "Even if you desire that they be guided, then verily Allah does not guide those whom He allowed to stray, and they will have no helpers." Another rendering has it: "Even though you, O Prophet, are keen on their guidance…"

Ibn Kathir sets it up as consolation: "Then Allah told His Messenger ﷺ that His eagerness to guide them will be of no benefit to them if Allah wills that they should be misguided." The ayah does not deny that eagerness. It takes it as given — and then sets its limit.

Ibn Kathir gathers the parallels. Allah says: *"And for whoever Allah wills to try with error, you can do nothing for him against Allah"* (5:41). And this burden is not new with our Prophet ﷺ — Nuh (peace be upon him) said the same to his people: *"And my advice will not profit you, even if I wish to give you good counsel, if Allah's will is to keep you astray"* (11:34). Also: *"Whomsoever Allah allows to stray, then there is no guide for him; and He lets them wander blindly in their transgressions"* (7:186), and *"Truly, those deserving the Word of your Lord will not believe, even if every sign should come to them — until they see the painful torment"* (10:96–97).

On the phrase **فَإِنَّ اللَّهَ** ("then verily, Allah"), Ibn Kathir comments: "this is the way in which Allah does things. If He wills a thing, then it happens, and if He does not will a thing, then it does not happen." And on **لَا يَهْدِي مَن يُضِلُّ**: "meaning the one whom He has caused to go astray, so who can guide him apart from Allah? No one."

Then the closing phrase, **وَمَا لَهُم مِّن نَّاصِرِينَ** — "and they will have no helpers" — which Ibn Kathir explains as: "they will have no one to save them from the punishment of Allah." He closes the passage with the ayah that settles the whole matter: *"Surely, His is the creation and the commandment. Blessed is Allah, the Lord of all that exists"* (7:54) — the creation is His, and so is the command.

## A question raised by ayah 36

Because ayah 36 says a messenger was sent to *every* community, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān pauses on a question its readers ask: did a messenger of Allah come to the lands now called India and Pakistan?

From this ayah, and from "there is no group of people among whom there has not been a warner" (35:24), Maʿārif says "it outwardly appears that messengers may have also been sent" to those regions — "whether residents of the area, or located in another country whose deputies or emissaries had reached there."

The apparent difficulty is 28:46, "so that you may warn a people unto whom came no warner," which seems to say the Prophet's ﷺ own people had received none. Maʿārif answers that this "obviously refers to the people of Arabia who became the first addressees of the prophetic mission" of the Prophet ﷺ — "the fact being that no prophet since Sayyidna Ismail (peace be upon him) had appeared among them," which is why the Qur'an gives them the title *Ummiyyīn*, the unlettered ones. "This does not necessarily imply that no prophet came before him in the rest of the world as well. Allah knows best." Note the restraint of that last phrase: the reading is offered, and the certainty handed back to Allah.

## Living it

**Never use the decree as a hiding place.** This is the passage's central discipline. When you catch yourself thinking *this is just how Allah made me*, or *if He didn't want it, it wouldn't be happening*, you are repeating the argument of ayah 35 in a softer voice. Ibn Kathir's answer stands: Allah's prohibition reached you "upon the tongue of His Messengers," and permission to act is not approval of the act.

**Do not invent religion.** Their second offence was declaring things forbidden with "no revealed authority" — and then attributing it to Allah. The safeguard is the same now as it was then: what Allah has forbidden is known from what He sent through His Messengers, not from custom, however old and however respectable.

**Convey clearly, then release the outcome.** Ayah 37 is medicine for anyone who aches over a family member who will not pray, or a friend who will not listen. The messengers themselves — including the Prophet ﷺ, and Nuh (peace be upon him) long before him — were told plainly that guidance is not in their hands. Your task is *al-balāgh al-mubīn*: to make it clear. Whether the heart opens is Allah's affair. That is not permission to stop caring; Ibn Kathir describes the Prophet's ﷺ eagerness for their guidance as a given. It is permission to stop carrying what was never yours.

**And keep asking Him.** Ibn Kathir's question hangs there: the one Allah has left to stray, "who can guide him apart from Allah? No one." If that is so, guidance is something to be begged for and never assumed — for the people we love, and first of all for ourselves.

passages.title: Their oaths denying resurrection are refuted
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** The idolaters thought that raising the dead was improbable, and they would not believe the Messengers who told them it would happen — so they swore by Allah, with their strongest oaths, that it never would. These three ayat take that oath apart. Ibn Kathir gives the whole movement in one line: "The Resurrection after Death is true, there is Wisdom behind it, and it is easy for Allah." Ayah 38 quotes the oath and answers it, ayah 39 gives the wisdom behind raising the dead, and ayah 40 shows how easy it is for Allah to do.

## The oath they swore

Ibn Kathir sets the scene plainly: "the idolators swore by Allah their strongest oaths, meaning that they made oaths swore fervently that Allah would not resurrect the one who died."

Two things there are worth pausing over.

**They swore by Allah.** Ibn Kathir calls them "the idolators" — and yet the name they swore by was Allah's. Their denial was not a denial that Allah exists. They knew His name well enough to use it as the seal on their sincerity, and then used that seal to deny what His Messengers had told them.

**"Their strongest oaths."** The translation renders the phrase "their most solemn oaths"; Ibn Kathir renders it "their strongest oaths" and describes them as swearing *fervently*. An oath is normally what a person reaches for when the argument is finished. Here there was never an argument to finish. Ibn Kathir tells us exactly what stood behind the swearing: "They considered that to be improbable, and did not believe the Messengers when they told them about that, swearing that it could not happen." No evidence — a sense of implausibility, and then oaths sworn all the more fervently to cover the gap. That is the shape of much denial: not a case, but an intensity.

## The one-word refutation

"Allah said, refuting them: **بَلَىٰ** (Yes), meaning it will indeed happen."

Notice how the answer has to be filled out in brackets to be read in English at all — "Yes, (He will raise them up)." A single word of the Qur'an carries the whole reply. Their most strenuous oaths are met, and settled, by it.

**"A promise binding upon Him in truth"** (*waʿdan ʿalayhi ḥaqqan*) — Ibn Kathir glosses this as "meaning it is inevitable." Read the wording carefully, because it is precious and could be misread. Nothing outside Allah lays obligations on Him; the same passage of Ibn Kathir ends by saying that "there is nothing that can stop Him or oppose Him." The resurrection is binding upon Allah because Allah has bound Himself to it by His own promise. It is as certain as His truthfulness — which is to say, absolutely certain. Their oath was a human attempt to make human words heavy. This is the promise of the One whose word is the heaviest thing there is.

**"But most of mankind know not."** Ibn Kathir: "because of their ignorance they oppose the Messengers and fall into disbelief." The diagnosis is ignorance, and it lands right beside their fervour. In one ayah we are shown people swearing with maximum confidence and people knowing nothing — and they are the same people. Certainty of tone and certainty of knowledge are not the same thing, and they can run in opposite directions.

## Ayah 39: why there has to be a Day

Having affirmed that it will happen, ayah 39 tells us *why*. Ibn Kathir introduces it exactly so: "Then Allah mentions His wisdom and the reason why He will resurrect mankind physically on the Day of Calling." The resurrection is not a display of raw power for its own sake. Two purposes follow, and the ayah states them both as purposes: "In order that He may make clear to them... and so that those who disbelieved may know..."

**First purpose: everything gets made clear.** "In order that He may make clear to them" — Ibn Kathir says this means "to mankind" — "what they differed over," which he explains as "every dispute." His gloss is as wide as it sounds. Every argument that history left hanging; every version of events that could never be checked; every quarrel where both sides went to the grave certain they were right. This world is very good at burying disagreements unresolved. The Day of Resurrection is where they are opened and settled by the One who was present for all of it. Ibn Kathir joins another ayah to this: "that He may requite those who do evil with that which they have done, and reward those who do good, with what is best" (53:31) — clarification and requital arriving together.

Two details in Ibn Kathir's sentence are worth catching. He says Allah will resurrect mankind **physically** — this is bodily resurrection, raised in the body. And he glosses "the Day of Calling" as the calling "between the people of Fire and of Paradise."

**Second purpose: the deniers will know what they were.** "And so that those who disbelieved may know that they were liars" — Ibn Kathir: "meaning that they lied in their oaths and their swearing that Allah would not resurrect those who die."

Feel the turn here. They swore they would never be raised. The moment that proves them liars is the moment they are standing there, raised. The very event they denied is both the courtroom and the evidence.

Ibn Kathir carries the scene through to its end: "they will be pushed down by force to the Fire with horrible force on the Day of Resurrection, and the guards of Hell will say to them: *This is the Fire which you used to belie. Is this magic or do you not see? Taste its heat, and whether you are tolerant of it or intolerant of it — it is all the same. You are only being requited for what you have done*" (52:14-16). Their own denial is quoted back to them. The words they were so sure of become the caption of their punishment.

## Ayah 40: "Be" — and it is

Ayah 39 answered *why*. Ayah 40 answers the objection buried under their oath: *how could He possibly?*

Ibn Kathir: "nothing is impossible for Him on earth or in heaven. When He wants a thing, all He has to do is say to it 'Be!' and it is. The Resurrection is one such thing; when He wants it to happen, all He will have to do is issue the command once, and it will happen as He wills."

He brings two ayat alongside it. "And Our commandment is but one, as the twinkling of an eye" (54:50) — one command, no duration. And "The creation of you all and the resurrection of you all are only as (the creation and resurrection of) a single person" (31:28) — the sheer numbers, which are exactly what made resurrection feel improbable to them, make no difference at all. Scale is a creaturely problem: more material, more time, more effort. Allah's act involves no effort to be multiplied.

**"When We intend it."** The ayah does not say that everything conceivable exists; it says that what Allah *intends* comes into being at His word. Power and will together — nothing happens by accident, and nothing He wills is delayed.

**"We issue the command once, and then it happens."** That is Ibn Kathir's gloss, and he draws out why once is enough: "Allah does not need to repeat or confirm whatever He commands, because there is nothing that can stop Him or oppose Him. He is the One, the Compelling, the Almighty, whose power, might and dominion have subjected all things."

And there is the quiet symmetry of the passage. They needed oath upon oath, strained to their strongest, to make their denial sound solid. He needs one word — *kun*, "Be!" — and it is. Repetition and insistence are what the weak reach for.

Ibn Kathir closes the passage where it was always heading: "None has the right to be worshipped except Him, and there is no Lord other than Him." That is not a change of subject. The One whose command works like this is the only One who deserves worship — which is precisely the point being pressed on people who swore by His name while worshipping others.

## A note from Maʿārif ul Qurʼān

Commenting in this section, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān takes up a question raised by ayah 36, just before our passage — "And We did raise a messenger among every people" — together with 35:24, "there is no group of people among whom there has not been a warner." Outwardly, the commentary says, these suggest that messengers may also have been sent to the areas now known as India and Pakistan, whether residents of those lands or emissaries who reached them from elsewhere. The apparent difficulty is 28:46, "so that you may warn a people unto whom came no warner." The answer given is that this refers to the people of Arabia, the first addressees of the mission of Sayyidnā Muḥammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ, among whom no prophet had appeared since Sayyidnā Ismāʿīl (peace be upon him) — which is why the Qur'an gives them the title *Ummiyyīn*, the unlettered ones. It does not necessarily follow that no prophet came to the rest of the world. And the commentary ends where such questions should end: **Allah knows best.**

This matters for our ayat. The idolaters' oath was not sworn in ignorance of any warning: Ibn Kathir says they "did not believe the Messengers when they told them about that" — and the verse quoted above says there is no group of people among whom there has not been a warner.

## Living it

**Guard your oaths, especially about what you cannot see.** They swore by Allah about the unseen, and their oath became the thing held against them. When a matter is genuinely beyond us, the honest answer is the one Maʿārif ul Qurʼān models: *Allah knows best.*

**Let ayah 39 settle your unsettled scores.** Every dispute will be made clear — including the ones nobody witnessed and you could never prove. You do not have to win every argument here, and you do not have to be believed here.

**Let ayah 40 shape your duʿāʾ** — your calling on Allah. If bringing a thing into being costs a single word, then the thing in your life you have privately filed as impossible is not hard for Him. That is a reason to keep asking.

**Take the promise as seriously as He states it** — *waʿdan ʿalayhi ḥaqqan*, a promise binding upon Him in truth. Ibn Kathir's word for it was: inevitable.

passages.title: Reward for those who emigrated under persecution
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These two ayat are Allah's answer to the believers who were driven out of their own city for their faith. Ayah 41 makes them two promises, one for this world and one for the next. Ayah 42 then names the qualities of the people who receive them: patience, and trust in their Lord.

Ibn Kathir reads them in exactly that order. Ayah 41 is the promise; then, in his words, "Allah describes them" — and ayah 42 is that description. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the link explicit: the two promises are made *subject to conditions*, and it draws those conditions out of the wording of both ayat together.

## The people these ayat are about

Ibn Kathir writes that Allah is telling us about the reward of those who migrated for His sake, seeking His pleasure — people who left their homeland behind, their brothers and their friends, hoping for the reward of Allah. He adds that this may have been revealed concerning those who migrated to Ethiopia: believers whose persecution at the hands of their own people in Makkah was so extreme that they left them and went to Ethiopia, simply so that they would be able to worship their Lord.

He names some of them. Among the most prominent of these emigrants were ʿUthmān ibn ʿAffān and his wife Ruqayyah, the daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; Jaʿfar ibn Abī Ṭālib, the cousin of the Messenger ﷺ; and Abū Salamah ibn ʿAbd al-Asad — among a group of almost eighty sincere and faithful men and women, may Allah be pleased with them all.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān agrees on the background: the occasion of revelation is basically that first hijrah to Ethiopia, with the probability that the words also take in the later hijrah to Madinah. So when you read ayah 41, picture a small band of roughly eighty people — including a daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — leaving for a foreign land because their own city had become a place where they could no longer worship their Lord.

Notice the wording of ayah 41: they emigrated **after they had been wronged** (*min baʿdi mā ẓulimū*). They were victims of injustice before they were emigrants. That detail matters for the promise that follows, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān will make it one of the conditions of the promise.

## Hijrah: what the word carries

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens with the verb itself. *Hājarū* comes from *hijrah*, which literally means to leave one's homeland. In Islam, leaving one's homeland for the sake of Allah is an act of great obedience and worship. The Prophet ﷺ said that hijrah demolishes all the sins that came before it — the migration wipes the slate clean.

Hijrah is obligatory (*farḍ*/*wājib*) in some situations and recommended (*mustaḥabb*) in others; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān refers the reader to its detailed treatment of the ayah in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ, *"Was not the earth of Allah wide enough that you might have sought refuge in it?"* — a question put to those who did not leave.

Then there is the phrase *fi'llāh* — "in Allah", rendered in our translation as "in the cause of Allah". Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats this as the very first condition attached to the promise: the purpose of the hijrah must be only to please Allah, with no selfish motive of material gain such as business or employment.

And the promise itself, in Ibn Kathir's rendering, is *la-nubawwi'annahum* — "We will **certainly** give them good residence in this world." They left their homes and their wealth, and what they are promised in return is a good place to live.

## "A good place in this world" — what it turned out to mean

Ibn Kathir records two readings of *fi'd-dunyā ḥasanah*:

- **Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Shaʿbī and Qatādah** said it means **al-Madīnah** — the city itself, the good residence Allah gave them.
- **Mujāhid** said it means **good provision** — sustenance, wealth, means.

Ibn Kathir then refuses to treat these as rivals: there is no contradiction between the two opinions, for they left their homes and their wealth, and Allah compensated them with something better in this world. Out of this he draws the principle that gives the passage its power: **whoever gives up something for the sake of Allah, Allah compensates him with something better for him than what he gave up** — and this is exactly what happened. Allah gave them power throughout the land and caused them to rule over the people, so they became governors and rulers, and each of them became a leader of the pious.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, quoting Qurṭubī, says the expression "a good place in the world" is highly comprehensive. It includes a good residence, and good neighbours; extended means of living; supremacy over hostile enemies; recognition and a fair name among people; and honour that continues through one's family and progeny.

Then it invites you to check the promise against history. Everyone saw how Madīnah was made for them the real good place to live. Instead of hostile neighbours they lived among people who were sympathetic, sharing and sacrificing. Enemies were conquered and subdued. Within a short period after the hijrah, doors of ample sustenance were thrown open to them; the poor and needy of former years became the wealthy citizens of the day. Many countries of the world came under their sway. And their moral greatness and beauty of conduct were such that they still receive words of praise from friends and foes alike, even to this day. Allah blessed them with great honour, and their generations after them.

That is the point of *"if they but knew"* at the end of ayah 41. Ibn Kathir explains it as: if only those who stayed behind and did not migrate with them knew what Allah had prepared for those who obeyed Him and followed His Messenger ﷺ. The regret in those words is aimed at the ones who stayed behind.

## "The reward of the Hereafter is greater"

Having listed what they received in this world — cities, provision, rule, honour — the ayah immediately puts it in its place. Ibn Kathir's gloss on *wa la-ajru'l-ākhirati akbar* is simply: greater than what We have given you in this world. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the greater reward of the Hereafter, which is limitless.

So the shape of ayah 41 is this: everything you can see, and then something larger than everything you can see. Madīnah, wealth, governorship, a name still praised by friends and foes to this day — and all of it is the smaller half of the promise.

## Ayah 42: the two qualities

Ibn Kathir reads ayah 42 as Allah's own description of these emigrants: *"those who remained patient, and put their trust in their Lord"* — meaning they bore their people's persecution with patience, putting their trust in Allah, who made their end good in this world and in the Hereafter.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the two ayat together into **four qualifications** on which the promise rests:

1. **"In Allah"** (*fi'llāh*) — the purpose of the hijrah must be only to please Allah, with no selfish motive of material gain such as business or employment.
2. **"After they were wronged"** (*min baʿdi mā ẓulimū*) — that these emigrants be genuine victims of injustice.
3. **"Those who were patient"** (*alladhīna ṣabarū*) — that they stay patient against the initial disadvantages and difficulties, showing steadfastness and fortitude.
4. **"And upon their Lord they place their trust"** (*wa ʿalā rabbihim yatawakkalūn*) — that even while utilising every available material means, they place their trust in Allah alone, because every ultimate success comes from Him alone.

That fourth point deserves a pause. *Tawakkul* — trust or reliance on Allah — is not here the abandonment of effort. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is explicit that the muhājir uses all available material means, and still places his trust in Allah alone rather than in the means.

## When the promise seems not to arrive

This is the most practically useful thing Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says about the passage. There are initial difficulties in everything one undertakes. So if a muhājir does not find the promised good place and favourable conditions, then instead of doubting the promise of the Qur'an, he should assess his own intention, sincerity and conduct — the very things on which the promises were made. Once he does that, he will discover that the fault was his own: perhaps the intention was not pure, or there was a lack of endurance and trust.

That is a strikingly honest instruction. The promise is not a mechanism triggered by changing address. It is tied to conditions, and a person who has not met them has no claim on it.

## Does the promise apply to us?

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān raises the question directly. Because the occasion of revelation was the emigration to Ethiopia (or to Madīnah), some scholars said the promise was for those blessed Companions only — and, as far as this world goes, it stood already fulfilled for them, something witnessed openly.

But it quotes Abū Ḥayyān in his *Tafsīr al-Baḥr al-Muḥīṭ*: the expression *"and those who migrated"* is general and inclusive of all those who leave their homeland, whatever their country or their time — so it takes in all the emigrants, from the very first of them down to the last among them who make hijrah for the sake of Allah, right up to the Day of al-Qiyāmah.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān endorses this on the basis of the general rule of tafsīr: **a commentator relies on the general sense of the wording, even though there be a particular event or group as the prime cause of the revelation.** Therefore the promise includes the emigrants of the whole world and of all times, and the fulfilment of both promises for all of them is certain. It notes a similar promise in Sūrat al-Nisāʾ: *"And whoever migrates in the way of Allah, he shall find many a place to settle and wide dimension (of resources)"* (4:100) — spaciousness of place and of means. But those deserving the fulfilment can only be the emigrants who possess these qualifications and have satisfied the conditions.

## Kinds of leaving — Qurṭubī's map

At this point Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reproduces a useful classification from Imām al-Qurṭubī, who quotes Ibn al-ʿArabī: going out of one's homeland and travelling through the earth is either **to run from something** and find a safe haven — this is what is properly called hijrah — or **to seek and get something**.

The flight kind has six categories:

1. **From a land of disbelief (*Dār al-Kufr*) to a land of Islam (*Dār al-Islām*).** This was obligatory in the Prophet's ﷺ own days and remains obligatory, subject to capability and ability, right through the Day of Qiyāmah — that is, where there is no security of life, property and honour, or where it is not possible to fulfil the religious obligations of the Dīn.
2. **Out of a place overtaken by innovation (*Dār al-Bidʿah*).** Ibn al-Qāsim reported hearing from Imām Mālik that it is not lawful for a Muslim to stay in a place where the righteous early generations of this community (*al-salaf al-ṣāliḥ*) are criticised and maligned. Ibn al-ʿArabī endorses this: if you cannot eradicate the practice of what is forbidden, then you must remove yourself from that place — as in the command, *"And when you see those who indulge in Our verses adversely, turn away from them"* (6:68).
3. **Out of a place overtaken by the unlawful (*ḥarām*)**, since the quest for what is lawful is an obligation on every Muslim.
4. **To avoid being subjected to physical harm.** This is permitted — indeed a blessing from Allah, that one should leave a place where he is in danger of being hurt. This kind of journey was first made by Ibrāhīm (peace be upon him), seeking deliverance from what his people inflicted on him; leaving Iraq for Syria he said, *"I am an emigrant unto my Lord"* (29:26). After him Mūsā (peace be upon him) made a similar journey from Egypt to Madyan, going out *"fearing, watching"* (28:21).
5. **Because of unsuitable climate or likely disease.** The Prophet ﷺ advised some shepherds to settle out by the groves outside Madīnah because the climate of the city did not suit them, and ʿUmar al-Fārūq (may Allah be pleased with him) sent an order to Abū ʿUbaydah to shift the provincial capital from Jordan to a site at higher altitude. But epidemics are governed by a different rule: those already present in the area do not leave it, and those outside do not go in. This is what happened when ʿUmar reached the borders of Syria and was told plague had spread there. He hesitated, and went into repeated consultations with the Companions, and the matter was resolved only when ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn ʿAwf narrated that the Prophet ﷺ said: *"When plague spreads in an area where you are present, do not go out from there; and when it spreads in an area where you are not already present, do not go in there."* (Reported by Tirmidhī, who calls it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ.) ʿUmar then proclaimed that the whole caravan would turn back. Some scholars have pointed out the particular wisdom in it: those staying in an affected area are most likely already infected, and one who fled would infect others wherever he went.
6. **To secure one's property and possessions**, when there is danger from thieves and robbers — for the property of a Muslim is as sacrosanct as his life.

The seeking kind, in Qurṭubī's list, has nine: travel for moral self-correction, i.e. touring Allah's earth to witness His creation and the manifestations of His power, and to observe the end of past peoples — *"Have they not travelled around the earth and seen how was the end of those before them?"* (35:44); the journey of Ḥajj; the journey of jihād; travel for employment, incumbent on one who cannot find economic support at home; travel for trading, permissible — Allah permits seeking His bounty even during the Ḥajj trip (2:198), so a journey for trade alone is permissible in the first degree; travel for education, an absolute duty in terms of religious need and an obligation of sufficiency (*farḍ al-kifāyah*, which if discharged by some suffices for others) beyond that; travel to a place believing it sacred and blessed, which Qurṭubī and Ibn al-ʿArabī restrict to the three mosques — al-Masjid al-Ḥarām, the Prophet's ﷺ Mosque in Madīnah, and al-Masjid al-Aqṣā (Mufti Muhammad Shafiʿ adds in a note that other revered scholars of early Islam and their successors did allow travel to visit places generally considered blessed); guarding the frontiers of Islam (*ribāṭ*); and travel to visit relatives and friends — a hadith of Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim mentions the prayer of the angels in favour of one who makes such a journey, valid only when the purpose is to seek the pleasure of Allah and not material gain. And Allah knows best.

## Living it

Three things this passage asks of a believer, and no more than that:

**Weigh what you give up against Who you are giving it to.** Ibn Kathir's principle is the heart of it: whoever gives up something for the sake of Allah, Allah compensates him with something better for him than that. They left their homes and their wealth, and the same people ended up governors and rulers, each of them a leader of the pious. Whatever you have surrendered for the sake of your Dīn — comfort, income, standing, a place you loved — is not lost with Allah.

**Do not read the promise as unconditional.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is insistent that the promises come with conditions, and that only those who satisfy them deserve the fulfilment: purity of intention, patience under the first difficulties, and trust in Allah while still using every available means. When the good place is slow to arrive, it tells you where to look first — at your own intention, sincerity and conduct, not at Allah's word.

**Keep the two rewards in proportion.** Ayah 41 grants that the worldly reward is real and was really given. Then it says the Hereafter is greater. Anyone who left something behind for Allah and has been paid back handsomely in this life is being told, gently, that he has so far received the smaller portion.

passages.title: Ask the people of knowledge about revelation
passages.tafsir:
**In one breath.** The Arabs — or some of them — objected that Allah was too great to send a human being as a Messenger. Ayah 43 answers by pointing at history: every messenger before Muhammad ﷺ was a man to whom Allah sent revelation — and if you do not know that, go and ask the people who do. Ayah 44 completes the thought: those men came with clear proofs and written Books, and the same pattern continues now, for Allah has sent down the Qur'an to this Prophet ﷺ so that he may explain it to people.

What holds the two ayat together is a single account of how revelation reaches humanity: through a human messenger, backed by evidence, carrying a Book, and explained by the one who received it.

## The objection behind the ayah

Ad-Dahhak reported from Ibn 'Abbas that when Allah sent Muhammad ﷺ as a Messenger, the Arabs — or some of them — denied him and said, "Allah is too great to send a human being as a Messenger." In response Allah revealed, *Is it a wonder to people that We have sent Our Inspiration to a man from among themselves (saying): "Warn mankind…"* (10:2), and then this ayah.

Ibn Kathir spells out the challenge it contains: ask the people of the previous Books — were the messengers sent to them human beings or angels? If they were angels, then you have a right to find this strange. But if they were human, you have no grounds to deny that Muhammad ﷺ is a Messenger.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, citing Rūḥ al-Maʿānī, adds a remarkable footnote to the episode: after the revelation of the verse, the Mushrikīn of Makkah actually sent emissaries to the Jews of Madinah to find out whether it was true that all earlier prophets had always been from among men. The Qur'an had put a question to them that could be checked — and they went and checked it.

That also explains why they were sent to non-Muslims. Maʿārif notes that the expression *ahl adh-dhikr* covers the People of the Book and the believers together, but the Mushrikīn were going to be satisfied only by the statement of non-Muslims. They were not satisfied with what the Prophet ﷺ himself was telling them — so how would they accept the statement of other Muslims?

## "Only men, to whom We sent revelation"

Ibn Kathir gathers a whole chorus of ayat on this theme, and it is worth hearing them one after another, because together they say something the objectors never expected:

- *And We sent not before you (as Messengers) any but men to whom We revealed, from among the people of townships* (12:109) — and, in Ibn 'Abbas's words, "not from among the people of heaven as you say."
- *Say: "Glorified be my Lord! Am I anything but a man, sent as a Messenger?" And nothing prevented men from believing when the guidance came to them, except that they said: "Has Allah sent a man as (His) Messenger?"* (17:93–94)
- *And We never sent before you any of the Messengers but verily, they ate food and walked in the markets* (25:20)
- *And We did not create them with bodies that did not eat food, nor were they immortals* (21:8)
- *Say: "I am not a new thing among the Messengers"* (46:9)
- *Say: "I am only a man like you. It has been revealed to me"* (18:110)

Notice what the objection actually was. It was not that the Prophet ﷺ was unimpressive; it was that he was *ordinary* — "a man from among themselves," as 10:2 puts it, one who ate food and walked through the markets. The Qur'an does not soften this. It insists on it. Eating food and walking in the markets is not an embarrassment to prophethood; it is the standing signature of it, in every age.

And the single clause that carries the whole weight is *nūḥī ilayhim* — "to whom We sent revelation." On the Qur'an's own testimony the prophets were not a different order of being; they were not immortal, and they were not from among "the people of heaven." The one thing that set them apart is that Allah sent revelation to them.

## Who are "the people of the dhikr"?

Maʿārif notes that in the phrase *ahl adh-dhikr* the word *dhikr* is used to carry more than one meaning. One of these is *ʿilm*, knowledge. It is in this sense, Maʿārif says, that the Qur'an identifies the Torah too as *dhikr* — *And verily We have written in the Zabūr, after the Dhikr* (21:105) — and similarly, in the very next statement of our own passage, *We sent down the Dhikr to you* (16:44), where *adh-dhikr* means the Qur'an. So *ahl adh-dhikr* literally means "the people of knowledge." The question is then: which people of knowledge? The scholars cited in our sources read it in three ways.

**The People of the Book.** Mujāhid reported from Ibn 'Abbas that *ahl adh-dhikr* means the People of the Book. Maʿārif takes the same view — attributing it to Ibn 'Abbas, Hasan and as-Suddiyy and others — and specifies the *scholars* among the Jews and Christians. This fits the setting exactly: the Makkans are being sent to the one community that had custody of the earlier prophetic history.

**The people of the Qur'an.** Others took *adh-dhikr* here in the same sense it carries in the very next ayah — the Qur'an — and so read *ahl adh-dhikr* as *ahl al-Qur'ān*, the people of the Qur'an.

**Whoever reliably knows the history of past nations.** Maʿārif calls this the clearest position, and attributes it to Rummānī, Zajjāj and Azharī: *ahl adh-dhikr* means the authentic historians of past peoples, whoever they may be — taking *dhikr* here in the sense of *ḥifẓ*, preserving and retaining. As though the ayah said: ask those who are genuinely informed about the reports of past communities, so that they may teach you. On this reading, Maʿārif notes, the phrase takes in both the People of the Book and the people of the Qur'an at once.

## Ayah 44: proofs and Books

**bi'l-bayyināt.** Ibn Kathir explains this as "proof and evidence." Maʿārif renders it as clear signs and miracles, and judges the sense of *miracles* more aptly applicable here. Either way, the messengers did not arrive with a bare claim; they arrived carrying credentials.

**wa'z-zubur.** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas, Mujāhid, Ad-Dahhāk and others that *zubur* is the plural of *zabūr*, meaning Scriptures, from the Arabs' expression *Zaburtul-Kitāb*, "I wrote the book" — and points to the Qur'an's own usage in *And everything they have done is noted in their Records* (54:52) and *And indeed We have written in az-Zabūr after the Dhikr that My righteous servant shall inherit the land* (21:105).

Maʿārif traces the word by a different route: *zubur* as the plural of *zubarah*, meaning large pieces of iron, as in *give me pieces of the iron* (18:96); because writing is a matter of putting pieces together, *zabar* came to mean writing and *az-zibr* a written book. The two derivations differ in path but converge in meaning: here it denotes the Book of Allah, and Maʿārif lists what that includes — Torah, Injīl, Zabūr and Qur'an.

So the shape of every prophetic mission was the same: a human messenger, evidence that he was sent, and a text.

## "And We sent down to you the Dhikr"

Ibn Kathir says plainly that *adh-Dhikr* in ayah 44 means the Qur'an; Maʿārif says this is so by consensus.

Then comes the purpose clause — *li-tubayyina li'n-nās mā nuzzila ilayhim*, "so that you may clearly explain to men what was revealed to them," i.e. sent down from their Lord. Ibn Kathir gives the reasons the task was entrusted to him ﷺ: "because you know the meaning of what Allah has revealed to you, and because of your understanding and adherence to it, and because We know that you are the best of creation and the leader of the Children of Adam."

And he defines what that explaining actually involves: **"so that you may explain in detail what has been mentioned in brief, and explain what is not clear."** That is a precise job description: where the revelation speaks in summary, his teaching supplies the detail; where it is not immediately clear, his words open it up.

## Why this ayah makes the Sunnah indispensable

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān builds a careful argument here. In this ayah the Prophet ﷺ is given the assignment of explaining the meaning of the revealed verses to people. Herein, it says, lies an open proof that a correct understanding of the realities, insights and injunctions of the Qur'an depends on his statement ﷺ. If everyone, simply by acquiring the knowledge of Arabic language and literature, were to become capable of understanding the injunctions of the Qur'an as Allah intended, then the mission of explaining assigned to him ﷺ would have been rendered meaningless.

Maʿārif then cites 'Allāmah Shāṭibī in *Al-Muwāfaqāt*, who provides detailed proof that the Sunnah of the Prophet ﷺ, the whole of it, is the explanation of the Book of Allah. The proof runs through the ayah *And surely you are at the height of a sublime nature* (68:4), which Sayyidah 'Ā'ishah explained by saying, "The Qur'an was his sublime nature." So every word and deed established from him ﷺ is, in the end, nothing but what the Qur'an said. Some of it is the express explanation of a verse of the Qur'an; some has no express mention in the Qur'an but rests nonetheless on a revelation that was not made part of the Qur'anic text — for *nor does he talk from desire; it is nothing but a revelation revealed* (53:3–4). And where he acted on his own *ijtihād* — his considered judgement — that too was ultimately corrected and supported, either through revelation or through the absence of any restraining order, and so stands empowered with the authority of revelation.

The final move is about preservation. Allah has said, *We, Ourselves, have sent down the Dhikr and We are there to protect it* (15:9). Now consider the great treasure of hadith which the Sahabah, the Tābiʿīn and the Muhaddithīn of the later period guarded more than their own lives — people who spent their whole lives sifting through that treasure, establishing the categories of narrations, separating out whatever they did not find of sufficient authority to base rulings upon, and writing standard books based exclusively on what proved correct and reliable after lifelong criticism and research. Maʿārif argues that if a person today calls that whole treasure unreliable under one pretext or another, he is committing himself to one of two claims: either the Prophet ﷺ did not carry out this Qur'anic command to explain, or he did explain and his explanation was not preserved for posterity. On either alternative, the Qur'an's *meaning* was left unprotected — which is contrary to Allah's own textual guarantee in 15:9. Hence its conclusion: whoever refuses the Sunnah as a binding authority of Islam is, in reality, a denier of the Qur'an itself. May Allah protect us from it.

## "Ask, if you do not know" — a rule for everyone

Maʿārif observes that although *So ask the people (having the knowledge) of the Message, if you do not know* appeared here in relation to one particular subject, its words are general and take in other matters of concern. Therefore, given the Qur'an's way with words, it lays down a genuinely important rule of procedure based on both reason and revelation: those who do not know the injunctions revealed for them should ask those who do, and act accordingly.

This, Maʿārif says, is what *taqlīd* — "to follow in trust" — is: one who does not know places his trust and confidence in someone who knows, accepts the ruling in question as the ruling of the Sharī'ah, and acts on it. Maʿārif notes that this rule has been in practice throughout the Muslim community from the age of the noble Sahabah to this day, and that even those who disavow taqlīd do not reject *this* form of it: that a person who is not a scholar takes a fatwā from the 'ulamā' and acts on it. And even when the scholar produces proof from Qur'an and Sunnah, an unversed questioner is still accepting that proof on the authority of, and trust in, the same scholar, since he does not himself have the ability to assess the arguments presented.

Maʿārif then distinguishes levels. Scholars who can themselves understand Qur'an and Hadith and know where consensus (*ijmāʿ*) lies are free to act directly on Qur'an, Hadith and ijmāʿ in matters clearly and explicitly stated in the texts, where no difference exists among the learned Sahabah and Tābiʿīn. But there are rulings not explicitly spelt out, or where the verses and narrations appear to conflict, or where the Sahabah and Tābiʿīn differed in determining their meaning — these are the objects of *ijtihād*, disciplined juristic reasoning. In these, Maʿārif holds, a scholar who does not possess the rank of *mujtahid* must still follow one of the Mujtahid Imams; relying on personal opinion, preferring one verse or narration and dismissing another as less weighty, is not permissible for him.

Deducing such rulings, Maʿārif continues, is the prerogative only of those Mujtahids who occupy the highest station of expertise in the Arabic language — its lexicography, idioms and modes of usage — who possess mastery over all the fields of knowledge related to Qur'an and Sunnah, and, above all, whose lives are marked by exemplary piety and mindfulness of Allah. It names Abū Ḥanīfah, Shāfiʿī, Mālik, Aḥmad ibn Ḥanbal, Awzāʿī and the jurist Abū'l-Layth and others like them as people Allah had specially blessed: they lived closer to the age of prophethood and of the Sahabah and Tābiʿīn, and under that *barakah* were given a special taste for the principles and objectives of the Sharī'ah. And it points out that figures of the calibre of al-Ghazālī, Rāzī, Tirmidhī, Ṭaḥāwī, Ma'zinī, Ibn Humām and Ibn Qudāmah — with all their own expertise — remained voluntarily within that following, weighing the Imams' sayings on the anvil of proofs from Qur'an and Sunnah and adopting whichever they found closest to them, but never departing from the approach of the Mujtahid Imams altogether.

This is Maʿārif's own considered position, and it is honest about the disagreement: it notes that Ibn Taymiyyah opposed taqlīd at large — while adding that even he rated one thing, in his *Fatāwā*, as forbidden by the consensus of the Ummah: picking and choosing among the Imams' rulings according to which is more conducive to one's worldly desire, which is following one's own desires under the cover of the Sharī'ah, a subject 'Allāmah Shāṭibī treats in great detail in *Al-Muwāfaqāt*.

It is to close that door, Maʿārif explains, that later-day jurists moved to *taqlīd shakhṣī* — "personal following," staying with one Imam consistently — and it offers two analogies. The first is Sayyidnā 'Uthmān al-Ghanī's restriction of what Maʿārif calls "the seven versions" of the Qur'an — the seven readings, *sabʿah aḥruf* — to a single version, with the total agreement of the noble Sahabah. All seven were genuine readings of the Qur'an, revealed through the angel Jibrā'īl as the Prophet ﷺ had wished; but when the Qur'an spread through non-Arab countries, the danger that it might be altered because of its seven readings became acute, so Muslims were instructed to write and recite one version only, and copies written accordingly were dispatched to various parts of the world. This never meant the other versions were untrue or inauthentic. (Maʿārif's own footnote, from Muhammad Taqi Usmani, flags that this whole discussion rests on 'Allāmah Ibn Jarīr's theory of the "Seven Versions.") The second analogy is homelier: a sick man is best served by settling on one physician rather than using one physician's prescription at one time and another's at another — which never implies that the other physicians are not experts.

And Maʿārif closes that discussion with a warning worth carrying: the reality of the Hanafī, Shāfiʿī, Mālikī and Hanbalī schools was no more than this functional arrangement, in which one still considers the other Imams worthy of the same respect. Giving it the touch of sectarianism and factionalism, or heating up mutual confrontation — scholarly research and debate becoming coloured with polemics, then reaching the level of blame and satire, then ignorance-based confrontation, until this state of affairs becomes the very indicator of being religious — is no valid mission of the revealed religion, and the discerning, far-sighted 'ulamā' never considered it good. *"So, before Allah is the complaint, and there is no strength and there is no power except with Allah, the High, the Great."*

## Where the passage lands

Ayah 44 does not end with the argument won; it ends with *wa laʿallahum yatafakkarūn* — "so that perhaps they may reflect." Ibn Kathir explains: they should examine themselves and be guided by it, so that they may attain the victory of salvation in this world and the next.

That is where the whole passage is aiming. It begins with people refusing a human messenger and ends by asking for something far simpler and far harder: that a person stop arguing long enough to think. Three things follow for us. Do not let ordinariness be an obstacle — Allah's guidance has always come through a human being who ate food and walked in the markets. When you do not know, ask someone who does; on Maʿārif's reading, ayah 43 makes that asking an explicit command of the Qur'an, not an admission of weakness. And read the Qur'an in the company of the one it was entrusted to, because by ayah 44 the explaining was part of the sending.

passages.title: Can the schemers feel safe from Allah?
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These three ayat ask one question and then refuse to let go of it: can people who quietly scheme evil ever really be *safe*? Ayah 45 opens the question, and ayat 46 and 47 extend it with "or… or…", laying out one route of seizure after another until no escape is left. Then, at the very end of ayah 47, the passage does something unexpected — it closes not with the blow but with mercy: "Indeed your Lord is full of kindness, Most Merciful."

## A warning moved forward in time

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān sets the context by looking back a few pages in the surah. At ayah 27 the deniers were told, "Then, on the Day of Judgment, He will put them to disgrace" — a warning about the Hereafter. Here in ayat 45–47 the warning is brought *forward*: it is entirely possible, Maʿārif explains, that they are seized by punishment from Allah right here in this world, long before the Hereafter — that the very ground they are sitting on swallows them, or that punishment reaches them from a direction they could never have imagined.

And Maʿārif points to a concrete fulfilment: **the Battle of Badr**. The Makkans were struck at the hands of what Maʿārif calls "some ragtag Muslims" arrayed against their thousand strong armed young men — a defeat they would never have perceived as possible. That is exactly the shape of the threat in ayah 45: the blow that arrives from where you were not watching.

## Who are "those who devise evil plots"?

Ibn Kathir frames the whole passage as a statement about **Allah's forbearance**. Allah, he says, is informing us about His patience, and how He delays the punishment of "the sinners who do evil things and call others to do likewise, plotting to call others to do evil" — even though He is fully able to make the earth swallow them or to bring His wrath upon them.

So the people described are not merely private wrongdoers. Their sin has a design to it and a reach: they *devise*, and the devising pulls other people in. And a plot, by its nature, is laid out of sight. Notice how the passage answers that in kind — if you scheme from where no one can see, know that Allah can seize you from where *you* cannot see (ayah 45).

## Four doors, and every one of them is open to Allah

**1. The ground itself (ayah 45).** That Allah "will cause them to sink into the earth" strikes at the one thing no one thinks to doubt — the floor beneath their feet. Ibn Kathir brings the parallel from Sūrat al-Mulk: "Do you feel secure that He Who is over the heaven (Allah), will not cause you to sink into the earth, when it quakes? Or do you feel secure that He Who is over the heaven (Allah), will not send a storm of stones upon you? Then you shall know how My warning really is" (67:16–17). *(As Ahl al-Sunnah, we affirm what Allah has affirmed of Himself in such verses as it came, without likening Him to His creation and without emptying the words of their meaning.)*

**2. "From where they do not perceive it" (ayah 45).** Ibn Kathir explains this as punishment arriving "in such a way that they do not know where it comes from." It is not only that the blow is sudden; it is that its direction cannot even be traced. There is no side to guard.

**3. "In the midst of their going to and fro" (ayah 46).** Ibn Kathir glosses this as being seized "when they are busy with their daily business, travel, and other distracting activities." **Qatadah and As-Suddi** said *taqallub* here means their journeys. Ibn Kathir supports it with Sūrat al-Aʿrāf: "Did the people of the towns feel secure against the coming of Our punishment by night while they were asleep? Or, did the people of the towns feel secure against the coming of Our punishment in the forenoon while they were playing?" (7:97–98). Maʿārif makes it ordinary and near: struck by a fatal disease, a fall from a height, or simply dying from colliding against something hard, all while roaming about freely.

Then comes the clause that shuts the last door: **فَمَا هُم بِمُعْجِزِينَ** — "so that there be no escape for them." Ibn Kathir's comment is blunt: "it is not impossible for Allah, no matter what their situation." Whatever the circumstance, however protected, they are not the ones who can frustrate Him.

**4. ʿalā takhawwuf (ayah 47)** — and here the passage turns on a single word that even the Companions had to stop and think about.

## The word that stopped ʿUmar

The word **تَخَوُّف (takhawwuf)** in ayah 47 is plainly built from **خَوف (khawf)** — fear, apprehension. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that the scholars read it in more than one way.

**Reading one — a punishment that spreads by dread.** Some commentators kept the plain sense of fear: one group is seized, which leaves a second group apprehensive; then the second group is seized, which leaves a third apprehensive — until, struck with dread one after another, the end comes for all of them.

Ibn Kathir's rendering runs along this line: "Or that He may punish them where they fear it most" — meaning Allah takes from them the very thing they most dread. And he adds the psychological point: this is even more frightening, "because when the thing you most fear to happen does happen, this is even worse." **Al-ʿAwfī reported that Ibn ʿAbbās** explained it as Allah saying: *If I wish, I can take him after the death of his companion and after he has become frightened of that.* Ibn Kathir notes the same was reported from **Mujāhid, Ad-Daḥḥāk, Qatādah and others**.

**Reading two — a punishment that works by shrinkage.** Maʿārif reports that **Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and other Imams of tafsir** took *takhawwuf* in the sense of **تَنَقُّص (tanaqquṣ)** — to decrease gradually. On this reading the punishment does not fall all at once.
