Instead, as Maʿārif describes it, "a general decrease sets in": wealth, health, fitness, means of sustenance, comfort and peace all go on shrinking, until the day comes when the people so punished disappear from the face of the earth for good. This is the sense behind the translation "destroy them gradually."

Both senses are traced back to early authorities. The fear-sense reaches us through Ibn Kathir, who reports it from Ibn ʿAbbās (by way of Al-ʿAwfī) and from Mujāhid, Ad-Daḥḥāk and Qatādah; the *tanaqquṣ*-sense reaches us through Maʿārif, which reports it from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and other Imams of tafsir. It is less a conflict than a word with two live senses, each describing a real way that Allah's grip closes.

**How ʿUmar settled it.** Maʿārif preserves a report from **Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab**, whom Maʿārif calls "the noble tābiʿī" — a *tābiʿī* being someone of the generation that came after the Prophet's ﷺ Companions. Sayyidnā **ʿUmar** himself hesitated over the meaning of this word. He addressed the Companions from the minbar and asked them what they understood *takhawwuf* to mean. The gathering fell silent. Then a man from the tribe of **Hudhayl** spoke up: "O Commander of the Faithful, this is a particular idiom of our tribe. We use this word in the sense of *tanaqquṣ* — to decrease gradually." ʿUmar pressed him: do the Arabs use it in that sense in their poetry? The man said they do, and recited a couplet of **Abū Kabīr al-Hudhalī**, a poet of his own tribe, in which the word carried exactly that meaning. ʿUmar then turned to the people and said: **"O people, learn about the poetry of Jāhiliyyah, because there lies the key to the explanation of your Book and the sense of your speech."**

Notice what the scene teaches before any conclusion is drawn from it. The Commander of the Faithful did not bluff; he asked. And the answer came from an ordinary tribesman who happened to know his own dialect.

**Two things Maʿārif draws out of this report:**

- **Casual Arabic is not enough to understand the Qur'an.** Being able to speak and write Arabic does not by itself qualify a person to understand revelation. What is needed is a level of competence and awareness that reaches back to the classical usage of the Arabs of the Jāhiliyyah — because the Qur'an was revealed in *that* language and *that* idiom. Maʿārif goes so far as to call learning Arabic literature at that level incumbent on Muslims.
- **Reading pre-Islamic poetry is permissible**, even though such poetry is inevitably full of pagan themes, customs, sayings and doings that run counter to Islam. Because the need — understanding the Qur'an — is so weighty, reading and teaching that poetry was declared permissible.

## Why a passage of threats ends in mercy

After four ways of being seized, ayah 47 lands on: **فَإِنَّ رَبَّكُمْ لَرَءُوفٌ رَّحِيمٌ** — "Indeed your Lord is full of kindness, Most Merciful." Why here?

**Ibn Kathir's answer:** precisely *because* He does not hasten to punish. The delay itself is the kindness. He cites what is reported in the Two Sahihs: *"No one is more patient in the case of hearing offensive speech than Allah, for they attribute to Him a son, while He alone is giving them provision and good health."* Read that against ayat 45–47: the same people plotting against Him are eating His provision and enjoying the health He gives them, and He does not strike.

But respite is not acquittal. Ibn Kathir immediately cites, also from the Two Sahihs: *"Allah will let the wrongdoer continue until, when He begins to punish him, He will never let him go."* The Messenger of Allah ﷺ then recited: "Such is the punishment of your Lord when He seizes the (population of) towns while they are doing wrong. Indeed, His punishment is painful, (and) severe" (11:102). Ibn Kathir adds: "And many a township did I give respite while it was given to wrongdoing. Then I punished it. And to Me is the (final) return (of all)" (22:48).

**Maʿārif's reading of the wording is finer still.** First, Allah says *your **Rabb*** — your Lord. The choice of that name, Maʿārif observes, hints that all these punishments which overtake people in this world are there **to warn them**, as part of the dictates of divine mercy. Second, *Raʾūf* is preceded by the emphatic **lām of taʾkīd** ("لَرَءُوفٌ") — stressing that Allah is *Very* Kind, *Very* Merciful. The hint, Maʿārif says, is that the warnings sent during the life of this world are in reality called for by His intrinsic kindness and mercy: they exist so that heedless men and women would learn from the warning and correct their deeds. Maʿārif titles this section pointedly — **even the punishment of this world is mercy in disguise**.

## Living it

**Do not read delay as permission.** The whole passage is aimed at a particular feeling — the settled sense of being safe. Nothing has happened, therefore nothing will. Ibn Kathir's framing removes the ground from under that feeling: the silence is Allah's patience, not His approval.

**Watch what your wrongdoing recruits.** Ibn Kathir specifies people who do evil *and call others to do likewise*. Influence multiplies a sin. Whatever you make normal for others, you carry.

**Take a decline seriously.** On the *tanaqquṣ* reading of ayah 47, a slow shrinking of health, provision, ease and peace can itself be the seizure. Maʿārif's own conclusion tells you what such a warning is *for*: not despair, but that a person learn from the warning and correct their deeds. A losing season is an invitation to return before the door narrows further.

**Learn the language properly.** ʿUmar's instruction from the minbar is a live one. Depth in Arabic — not conversational fluency, but the classical usage the Qur'an was revealed in — is a key to the Book.

**Hold the two ends together.** Ayat 45–47 do exactly that: four hammer blows of possibility, and then the reminder that your Lord is Raʾūf, Raḥīm. Fear without that ending becomes despair; the ending without that fear becomes carelessness. The passage gives you both in a single breath.
